items.q: What is the net primary productivity (NPP) of the grasses?
options: 15,000 kcal/m²/yr
33,000 kcal/m²/yr
2,400 kcal/m²/yr
9,000 kcal/m²/yr

why.correct: NPP is GPP minus the producers' own respiration: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>24</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">24{,}000 - 9{,}000</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>kcal/m</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>/yr</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 15{,}000\,\text{kcal/m}^2\text{/yr}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: Right: GPP minus respiration.
This adds respiration to GPP; respiration is energy the grasses use up, so it is subtracted.
This applies the 10% rule to GPP; the 10% rule is for passing energy to consumers, not for NPP.
This is the energy used in respiration, not what is left after it.

items.q: About how much energy from the grasses' NPP reaches the secondary consumers?
options: 1,500 kcal/m²/yr
150 kcal/m²/yr
15 kcal/m²/yr
240 kcal/m²/yr

why.correct: Secondary consumers are two steps above the producers, so apply 10% twice: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>0.10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>0.10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15{,}000 \times 0.10 \times 0.10</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>150</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>kcal/m</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>/yr</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 150\,\text{kcal/m}^2\text{/yr}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: This is one step, the primary consumers. Secondary consumers are one more step up.
Right: two steps of 10% from the NPP.
This is three steps of 10%, the tertiary consumers.
This starts from GPP instead of NPP; consumers can eat only what the producers store, the NPP.

items.q: Why does so little of the producers' energy reach the secondary consumers?
options: Decomposers recycle most of the energy back to the grasses
Consumers store most of the energy they eat as new body tissue
At each level most energy is used in respiration and lost as heat
Energy is destroyed each time one organism eats another

why.correct: At each trophic level most of the energy is used for life processes and lost as heat, and some is never eaten or digested, so only about 10% passes up.
options: Energy flows one way and leaves as heat; nutrients are recycled, energy is not.
Only about 10% becomes new tissue; most is used in respiration.
Right: respiration turns most of the energy into heat at every level.
Energy is not destroyed; it is converted, mostly to heat.

items.q: Two islands lie the same distance from the mainland. Island A covers 10 km² and Island B covers 1,000 km². What does the theory of island biogeography predict?
options: Island A has more species, since small islands are easier for colonists to reach
Both islands have the same number of species, since they are equally far from the mainland
Island B has fewer species, since larger islands support more predators
Island B has more species, since it has more habitats and lower extinction rates

why.correct: With distance the same, area decides: a larger island has more kinds of habitat and larger populations, so fewer species go extinct and more species persist.
options: The islands are the same distance away, so they are equally easy to reach; size is what differs.
Distance is only one factor; island size also sets species richness.
Predators do not make large islands poorer in species; more habitat supports more species.
Right: more habitat, lower extinction.

items.q: A student wants to test whether water temperature changes how many mayfly larvae survive. Which is a testable hypothesis?
options: Does water temperature change how many mayfly larvae survive?
If water is warmer than 25 °C, then fewer mayfly larvae will survive to adulthood.
Water temperature has an effect on mayfly larvae.
Mayfly larvae prefer cooler streams because they like them better.

why.correct: A testable hypothesis is a statement that names the change and predicts the direction of the measured result: warmer water, fewer larvae surviving.
options: A question is not a hypothesis; it makes no prediction to test.
Right: a directional, testable statement.
"Has an effect" gives no direction, so no result could show it wrong.
Preference is not what is measured, and "because they like them" explains nothing.

items.q: An oyster releases millions of eggs, and most of its larvae die within days. Which survivorship curve does the oyster show?
options: Type III: steep early losses, then a flatter line for the few survivors
Type I: low death rates until old age, then a steep drop
Type II: a steady death rate at each age
K-selected: few offspring with heavy parental care

why.correct: Heavy losses among the very young, with a few survivors living on, make a Type III curve.
options: Right: a steep fall at the start of life.
Type I fits species such as humans, where most live to old age.
Type II has the same chance of dying at any age, as in many birds.
This is a reproductive strategy, not a survivorship curve, and it is the opposite of the oyster's.

items.q: Deer on an island rose from 50 to 2,000 in 15 years, then fell to 400 after a hard winter. The island's shrubs were heavily browsed. Which explanation fits best?
options: The carrying capacity rose, so the herd had room to keep growing
The herd overshot the carrying capacity, overgrazed its food, then died back
The herd leveled off smoothly at the carrying capacity, as in logistic growth
Births stopped because the herd reached replacement-level fertility

why.correct: The herd grew past what the island could support, ate the shrubs faster than they regrew, and starved when food ran short: overshoot and dieback.
options: A rising carrying capacity would not cause a crash, and browsed shrubs mean less food.
Right: overshoot, overgrazing, dieback.
A logistic curve levels off; this herd crashed.
Replacement-level fertility describes human populations, and it would not cause a sudden fall.

items.q: What was Country P's rate of natural increase in 2025, in percent per year?

why.correct: Subtract the death rate from the birth rate and divide by 10 to turn a rate per 1,000 into a percent: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>28</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mn>10</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{28 - 8}{10} = 2.0\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: Right: (CBR minus CDR) divided by 10.
This is the difference per 1,000 people; divide by 10 to get percent.
This divides by 100; rates per 1,000 become percent by dividing by 10.
This adds the death rate to the birth rate; deaths are subtracted.

items.q: If Country P keeps its 2025 rate of natural increase, in about what year will its population reach 80 million?

why.correct: 80 million is double 40 million. The rule of 70 gives a doubling time of <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>÷</mo><mn>2.0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">70 \div 2.0 = 35</annotation></semantics></math> years, and <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2025</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2060</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2025 + 35 = 2060</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: This uses 20 as the growth rate (the rate per 1,000), giving a doubling time of 3.5 years.
This adds the death rate to the birth rate (3.6%) before using the rule of 70.
Right: 35 years after 2025.
This adds 70 years without dividing by the growth rate.

items.q: Based on the table, which stage of the demographic transition is Country P most likely in?
options: Stage 1: birth and death rates are both high
Stage 2: death rates fall while birth rates stay high
Stage 3: birth rates are falling toward low death rates
Stage 4: birth and death rates are both low and close

why.correct: The death rate was already low (9, then 8) while the birth rate fell from 40 to 28: a falling birth rate approaching a low death rate is stage 3.
options: Stage 1 has high death rates; Country P's death rate is low.
In stage 2 the birth rate stays high; Country P's fell by 12 per 1,000.
Right: birth rates falling toward low death rates.
A birth rate of 28 is still far above the death rate of 8, so the population is still growing quickly.

items.q: A town's planners map the area of land whose rain and snowmelt drain into the town's river. What are they mapping?
options: An aquifer, the porous rock that holds groundwater
A watershed, the land that drains into one body of water
An estuary, where the river meets the sea
The water table, the top of the saturated ground

why.correct: A watershed is all the land that drains to one river, lake or other body of water.
options: An aquifer is underground rock or sediment that holds water, not an area of land that drains.
Right: a watershed.
An estuary is where fresh and salt water mix at a river's mouth.
The water table is a level underground, not an area of land.

items.q: During an El Niño year, which change happens off the coast of Peru?
options: Trade winds strengthen and pull more cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface
Upwelling increases, so the anchovy catch rises
Trade winds weaken and upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water declines
Sea ice forms along the coast and cools the air

why.correct: In El Niño the trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east, and the cold upwelling off Peru weakens, so nutrients and fish decline.
options: Stronger trade winds and more upwelling describe La Niña.
Upwelling declines in El Niño, and the anchovy catch falls.
Right: weaker winds, less upwelling.
The coast of Peru is tropical; sea ice is not part of El Niño.

items.q: A city wants to reduce street flooding downtown after storms, but it cannot buy any new land. Which solution fits?
options: Build a new reservoir on farmland outside the city
Line downtown streams with concrete so water moves away faster
Add storm drains that carry runoff straight to the river
Replace parking-lot pavement with permeable pavement that lets rain soak in

why.correct: Permeable pavement lets rain soak into the ground where it falls, on land the city already uses, so less water runs off into the streets.
options: A new reservoir needs land the city cannot buy.
Concrete channels speed water downstream and add to flooding there; they do not reduce runoff.
More drains move the same runoff faster, carrying its pollutants to the river.
Right: it cuts runoff on land the city already has.

items.q: How much electricity does the school save in one year?
options: 34 kWh

why.correct: Each tube saves <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32 - 15 = 17</annotation></semantics></math> W. Then <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>400</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>17</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>W</mtext><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>h</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">400 \times 17\,\text{W} \times 2{,}000\,\text{h}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>600</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 13{,}600{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> Wh, and dividing by 1,000 gives <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>600</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">13{,}600</annotation></semantics></math> kWh.
options: This is the saving in watt-hours; divide by 1,000 for kilowatt-hours.
This is the energy the new LED tubes use, not the saving.
This is the saving for one tube; multiply by the 400 tubes.
Right: the power saved times the hours, in kWh.

items.q: How much money does the school save on electricity in one year?

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>600</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>kWh</mtext><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>0.12</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>kWh</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">13{,}600\,\text{kWh} \times \frac{$0.12}{1\,\text{kWh}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>632</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= $1{,}632</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: Right: kWh saved times the price per kWh.
This divides by the price; multiply so the kWh cancel.
This is the yearly cost of the old tubes, not the saving.
This is the yearly cost of the new LED tubes, not the saving.

items.q: How much carbon dioxide does the upgrade keep out of the air each year?

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>600</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>kWh</mtext><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>0.4</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>kg</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>kWh</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">13{,}600\,\text{kWh} \times \frac{0.4\,\text{kg}}{1\,\text{kWh}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>440</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>kg</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 5{,}440\,\text{kg}</annotation></semantics></math> of carbon dioxide.
options: This divides by the emission factor; multiply so the kWh cancel.
This uses the LED tubes' energy, not the energy saved.
Right: kWh saved times kg per kWh.
This divides by 1,000 a second time; the saving is already in kWh.

items.q: A lake downwind of a coal-burning region has become more acidic. Which pair of pollutants is chiefly responsible?
options: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides
Carbon dioxide and methane
Chlorofluorocarbons and ozone
Particulate matter and volatile organic compounds

why.correct: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides react with water in the air to form sulfuric and nitric acids, which fall as acid deposition.
options: Right: SO2 and NOx form the acids.
These trap heat; they are not the main cause of acid deposition.
These are tied to the ozone layer and smog, not acid deposition.
These cause haze and smog rather than acid deposition.

items.q: Pesticide X has an LD50 of 50 mg/kg in rats, and pesticide Y has an LD50 of 500 mg/kg. Which statement is correct?
options: Pesticide Y is 10 times as toxic as pesticide X
Pesticide X is 10 times as toxic as pesticide Y
Pesticide X is 450 times as toxic as pesticide Y
The two are equally toxic, since both kill half the rats

why.correct: A lower LD50 means a smaller dose kills half the test animals, so X is more toxic: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>500</mn><mo>÷</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">500 \div 50 = 10</annotation></semantics></math> times as toxic.
options: This reverses the rule; a higher LD50 means a less toxic substance.
Right: 500 divided by 50.
This subtracts the LD50s; compare them by dividing.
Both kill half at their LD50, but X does it at a tenth of the dose.

items.q: Which statement correctly tells the greenhouse effect apart from ozone depletion?
options: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared leaving Earth; stratospheric ozone absorbs incoming ultraviolet
Greenhouse gases absorb incoming ultraviolet; ozone absorbs outgoing infrared
The ozone hole lets heat escape to space, which causes global warming
Carbon dioxide breaks down ozone, which lets more heat reach the surface

why.correct: Greenhouse gases trap outgoing infrared radiation and warm the lower atmosphere; the stratospheric ozone layer absorbs incoming ultraviolet radiation. They are different processes.
options: Right: infrared for the greenhouse effect, ultraviolet for the ozone layer.
This swaps the two kinds of radiation.
The ozone hole lets in more ultraviolet; it is not the cause of global warming.
Carbon dioxide does not destroy ozone; CFCs do.

items.q: Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere rose from 316 ppm in 1959 to 420 ppm in 2023. What was the percent change?
options: About 25%
About 33%
About 104%
About 1.3%

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>420</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>316</mn></mrow><mn>316</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{420 - 316}{316} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">≈</mo><mn>33</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 33\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: This divides by the new value, 420; percent change divides by the old value.
Right: the change over the old value, times 100.
This is the change in ppm, 104, not a percent.
This is the ratio of new to old, 1.33, without subtracting 1 and multiplying by 100.

items.q: Which change would raise global sea level?
options: Melting of floating Arctic sea ice
More carbon dioxide dissolving in seawater
Melting of the Greenland ice sheet, which sits on land
A thicker ozone layer in the stratosphere

why.correct: Ice on land adds new water to the ocean when it melts. Floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water, so its melting barely changes sea level.
options: Floating ice already displaces its weight in water, so melting it adds almost nothing.
Dissolved carbon dioxide lowers the ocean's pH; it does not raise sea level.
Right: melting land ice adds water to the ocean.
The ozone layer has no direct effect on sea level.

items.q: A migratory bird is declining because the wetlands where it rests are being drained. Which response is a policy?
options: Satellite tags that track the birds' migration routes
A law that protects the wetlands where the birds stop to feed and rest
A captive breeding program that raises chicks at a zoo
A yearly survey that counts the birds each spring

why.correct: A policy is a law or rule. Protecting the stopover wetlands by law also treats the cause, the loss of habitat.
options: Tracking is a technology for research; it does not protect habitat.
Right: a law that protects the habitat.
Captive breeding is a management action, not a law or rule, and it leaves the habitat loss in place.
A survey measures the decline; it is monitoring, not a policy.

items.q: Which change moves carbon from a long-term reservoir into the atmosphere the fastest?
options: Burning coal in a power plant
Photosynthesis by a growing forest
Limestone forming on the sea floor
Dead plants being buried in a peat bog

why.correct: Coal is carbon stored for millions of years; burning releases it as carbon dioxide in moments.
options: Right: combustion of fossil carbon.
Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air.
Forming limestone stores carbon, slowly.
Burial in a bog stores carbon; it does not release it.

items.q: Soil bacteria turn the ammonium in a fertilizer into nitrate that crops take up. Which process is this?
options: Nitrogen fixation
Denitrification
Nitrification
Ammonification

why.correct: Nitrification is the bacterial conversion of ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate.
options: Nitrogen fixation turns nitrogen gas into ammonia or ammonium.
Denitrification turns nitrate back into nitrogen gas.
Right: ammonium to nitrate.
Ammonification turns the nitrogen in dead matter and wastes into ammonium.

items.q: A town is deciding whether to drain a wetland to build homes. Which ecosystem service would the town most likely lose?
options: Flood control, as the wetland stores storm water and releases it slowly
Timber, as the new lots would have more trees to sell
Tax revenue, as homes would pay less tax than the wetland
Mosquito control, as wetlands keep mosquito numbers low

why.correct: Wetlands soak up storm water like a sponge and release it slowly, a regulating service the town loses if it drains them.
options: Right: flood control is a regulating service of wetlands.
Clearing for homes removes plants; it does not add timber.
Homes usually add tax revenue; that is not a service the wetland provides.
Standing water in wetlands is where mosquitoes breed, so this is not the service lost.

items.q: After a forest fire, the soil remains, and grasses and shrubs appear within a year. Which describes this?
options: Primary succession, since pioneer species move in first
Primary succession, since the fire removed the trees
Secondary succession, since lichens first break down the rock
Secondary succession, since the soil was left in place

why.correct: Succession that starts where soil already exists, after a disturbance such as fire, is secondary succession.
options: Pioneer species appear in both kinds; what decides is whether soil remains.
Removing trees does not make it primary; the soil is still there.
Breaking down bare rock is how primary succession starts.
Right: soil remains, so it is secondary succession.

items.q: Which set of traits describes a K-selected species?
options: Many small offspring, short lives, little parental care
Few offspring, long lives, much parental care
Heavy early losses shown by a Type III curve
Rapid growth after a disturbance, then a crash

why.correct: K-selected species have few offspring, invest heavily in each, live long, and tend to stay near carrying capacity.
options: These are r-selected traits.
Right: few offspring, much care, long lives.
This is a survivorship curve, and it fits r-selected species.
Boom and bust after a disturbance is typical of r-selected species.

items.q: What was the percent change in the city's population from 2000 to 2025?

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>500</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>200</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>200</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1{,}500{,}000 - 1{,}200{,}000}{1{,}200{,}000} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 25\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: This divides by the 2025 value; divide by the old value, 1,200,000.
Right: the change over the old value, times 100.
This forgets to multiply by 100.
This is the new value as a percent of the old; subtract the old value first.

items.q: If the city keeps growing at 1.4% per year, in about what year will its population reach 3,000,000?

why.correct: 3,000,000 is double the 2025 population. The rule of 70 gives <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>÷</mo><mn>1.4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">70 \div 1.4 = 50</annotation></semantics></math> years, and <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2025</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2075</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2025 + 50 = 2075</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: This uses 14 instead of 1.4 for the growth rate.
This adds the doubling time to 2000; the 1.4% rate and the 1,500,000 start in 2025.
Right: 50 years after 2025.
This adds 70 years without dividing by the growth rate.

items.q: If the city's growth rate fell from 1.4% to 0.7% per year, how would its doubling time change?
options: It would halve, to about 25 years
It would stay at about 50 years, since the population is the same
It would fall by 0.7 years
It would double, to about 100 years

why.correct: Doubling time is 70 divided by the growth rate, so halving the rate doubles the time: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>÷</mo><mn>0.7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">70 \div 0.7 = 100</annotation></semantics></math> years.
options: Halving the rate makes growth slower, so doubling takes longer, not shorter.
Doubling time depends on the growth rate, not on the population size.
The rule of 70 divides; it does not subtract.
Right: half the rate, twice the doubling time.

items.q: A country's population pyramid has a wide base that narrows steadily toward the top. What does it predict?
options: Rapid growth, since many young people will soon reach childbearing age
Zero growth, since each age group replaces the one above it
Slow growth, since most people are past childbearing age
A shrinking population, since few people reach old age

why.correct: A wide base means a large share of children; as they reach childbearing age, births stay high and the population keeps growing.
options: Right: a young population grows fast.
Zero growth shows as a column-shaped pyramid with similar-sized age groups.
A wide base means most people are young, not past childbearing age.
A narrow top reflects high death rates in the past, but the large young groups mean growth ahead.

items.q: Which soil holds the most water but lets water drain through it slowly?
options: A sandy soil, with large particles and large pores
A soil made mostly of gravel and coarse sand
A clay soil, with tiny particles and tiny pores
A loose soil with large pores between its grains

why.correct: Clay's tiny particles leave tiny pores: water moves through them slowly but is held tightly.
options: Large pores let water drain quickly, so sand holds little.
Gravel drains fastest and holds the least water.
Right: small pores hold water and slow drainage.
Large pores mean high permeability and low water holding.

items.q: Moist air from the ocean rises over a mountain range. What is the climate on the far (leeward) side most likely to be?
options: Wet, since the air cools and condenses as it sinks
Dry, since the air dropped its moisture as rain while rising
Wet, since sinking air carries ocean moisture over the peaks
Dry, since the mountains block sunlight from that side

why.correct: Rising air cools and its water vapor condenses into rain on the windward side; the dry air then sinks and warms on the leeward side, making a rain shadow.
options: Sinking air warms, which keeps water vapor from condensing.
Right: a rain shadow.
The moisture fell on the windward side; the air that crosses is dry.
Rain shadows come from moisture loss, not from a lack of sunlight.

items.q: How much water per hectare would drip irrigation use?

why.correct: 40% less means 60% of the flood amount: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>m</mtext><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>0.60</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6{,}000\,\text{m}^3 \times 0.60</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>600</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>m</mtext><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 3{,}600\,\text{m}^3</annotation></semantics></math> per hectare.
options: This is the 40% saved, not the 60% still used.
This subtracts 40 cubic meters instead of 40%.
This adds 40% instead of taking it away.
Right: 60% of 6,000.

items.q: How much water would the whole 40-hectare farm save in one season by switching to drip irrigation?

why.correct: Each hectare saves <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>600</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6{,}000 - 3{,}600</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>400</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>m</mtext><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 2{,}400\,\text{m}^3</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>400</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>m</mtext><mn>3</mn></msup><mtext>/ha</mtext><mo>×</mo><mn>40</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>ha</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2{,}400\,\text{m}^3\text{/ha} \times 40\,\text{ha}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>96</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>m</mtext><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 96{,}000\,\text{m}^3</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: Right: the saving per hectare times 40 hectares.
This is the water drip irrigation would use, not the water saved.
This is the water flood irrigation uses on the whole farm.
This is the saving for one hectare; multiply by 40.

items.q: How much money would the farm save on water in one season?

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>96</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>m</mtext><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>0.25</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>m</mtext><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">96{,}000\,\text{m}^3 \times \frac{$0.25}{1\,\text{m}^3}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= $24{,}000</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: This divides by the price; multiply so the cubic meters cancel.
Right: the water saved times the price.
This is the cost of the water drip irrigation would still use.
This is the cost of flood irrigation for the whole farm.

items.q: A coal plant turns 35% of its fuel's energy into electricity, the power lines lose 10% of that electricity, and a motor is 90% efficient. About what share of the coal's energy becomes useful work in the motor?
options: About 72%
About 15%
About 35%
About 28%

why.correct: Efficiencies in a chain multiply: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.35</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>0.90</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>0.90</mn><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.28</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.35 \times 0.90 \times 0.90 \approx 0.28</annotation></semantics></math>, about 28%.
options: This averages the three percents; a chain multiplies them.
This subtracts the losses from 35%; multiply the efficiencies instead.
This is the plant alone; the lines and the motor lose more.
Right: the product of the efficiencies.

items.q: Which is a drawback of nuclear power plants?
options: They release large amounts of carbon dioxide while running
Their steam is a major source of acid deposition
Spent fuel stays radioactive for thousands of years and needs secure storage
Their fuel is water, which they use up

why.correct: Spent fuel rods stay dangerously radioactive for thousands of years, and long-term storage is still an unsolved problem.
options: Running nuclear plants release almost no carbon dioxide.
The steam is water vapor; it does not cause acid deposition.
Right: long-lived radioactive waste.
The fuel is uranium; water is used for cooling and steam.

items.q: On a sunny summer day in a large city, when is ground-level ozone usually highest?
options: During the morning rush hour, when cars give off ozone directly
Around midnight, when the air is coolest
Mid-afternoon, after hours of sunlight act on nitrogen oxides and VOCs
At dawn, before sunlight reaches the streets

why.correct: Ozone is a secondary pollutant: sunlight drives reactions of the morning's nitrogen oxides and VOCs, so ozone builds through the day and peaks in mid-afternoon.
options: Cars give off nitrogen oxides and VOCs, not ozone; ozone forms later in sunlight.
Without sunlight, ozone formation stops and ozone levels fall at night.
Right: sunlight plus the morning's emissions.
There is little sunlight at dawn, so little ozone has formed.

items.q: During a thermal inversion, why do pollutants stay trapped near the ground?
options: A layer of warm air above cooler surface air keeps the surface air from rising and mixing
A layer of cold air above warm surface air pushes the pollutants down
Strong winds press the pollutants against the ground
Rain washes the pollutants out of the upper air into the valley

why.correct: Normally air cools with height and warm surface air rises. In an inversion, warmer air sits on top, so the cool surface air cannot rise and pollutants build up.
options: Right: warm air over cool air stops mixing.
This is the normal pattern, which lets air rise and mix; an inversion is the reverse.
Inversions come with calm air; wind would mix and clear the pollutants.
Rain cleans pollutants out of the air; it does not trap them.

items.q: DDT in plankton measures 0.04 ppm, and its concentration rises about 10 times at each step up a food chain. What is the expected concentration in an eagle three steps above the plankton?
options: 40 ppm
4 ppm
0.4 ppm
1.2 ppm

why.correct: Multiply by 10 once per step: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.04</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>ppm</mtext><mo>×</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.04\,\text{ppm} \times 10 \times 10 \times 10</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>40</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>ppm</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 40\,\text{ppm}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: Right: three steps of 10 times.
This is two steps, not three.
This is one step.
This multiplies by 10 and then by 3; each step multiplies by 10 again.

items.q: What was the average rate of sea level rise from 1993 to 2023?
options: About 3.4 mm per year
About 34 mm per year
About 3.7 mm per year
About 0.29 mm per year

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>103</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>mm</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>mm</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>2023</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1993</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{103\,\text{mm} - 0\,\text{mm}}{2023 - 1993}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>103</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>mm</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>30</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>yr</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{103\,\text{mm}}{30\,\text{yr}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">≈</mo><mn>3.4</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>mm/yr</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 3.4\,\text{mm/yr}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: Right: the rise over 30 years.
This divides by 3 decades but reports it per year; that is the rise per decade.
This is the rate for the last decade alone, 2013 to 2023.
This divides the years by the rise; the rate is rise over time.

items.q: Which statement best describes the trend in the table?
options: Sea level rose a steady 32 mm in each decade
Sea level rose until 2013 and then fell
Sea level rose fastest from 1993 to 2003
Sea level rose in each decade, and the rise per decade grew

why.correct: The rises per decade were 32, 34 and 37 mm: sea level rose each decade, a little faster each time.
options: The rise per decade was 32, then 34, then 37 mm, so it was not steady.
The value grew from 66 to 103 mm after 2013.
The first decade had the smallest rise, 32 mm.
Right: 32, 34, then 37 mm per decade.

items.q: Which two processes are the main causes of the rise in sea level shown?
options: Melting of floating sea ice, and more rain over the oceans
Seawater expanding as it warms, and melting glaciers and ice sheets on land
More dissolved carbon dioxide expanding seawater, and melting sea ice
Thinning of the ozone layer, and more evaporation from the oceans

why.correct: Warmer water takes up more room (thermal expansion), and melting land ice adds water to the ocean.
options: Floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water, and rain over the ocean is water already in the cycle.
Right: thermal expansion and land ice.
Dissolved carbon dioxide lowers pH; it does not expand seawater.
The ozone layer does not control sea level, and evaporation removes water from the ocean.
